summary: This RFC defines additional CDNI Capability Objects giving the delegating upstream CDN information on a downstream CDN's current utilization and usage limits. That helps the upstream CDN decide how much traffic to delegate. It supplements RFC 8008.

eli5.summary: One delivery company asks a partner how busy it is before handing over more parcels. This defines the messages for sharing that.

questions: how does a ucdn know dcdn load
what is the difference between maximum hard and maximum soft
how does a ucdn track dcdn usage
subtitle: How a downstream CDN tells its upstream partner how much traffic it can take, and where to watch the numbers.

tldr.problem: When one content delivery network (the uCDN) hands traffic to a partner network (the dCDN), it needs to know how much is too much, and both sides need to measure usage the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The dCDN advertises two new Capability Objects: FCI.CapacityLimits, which states hard and soft limits such as bits per second, and FCI.Telemetry, which points to near real-time metrics that track usage against those limits.
tldr.outcome: The uCDN can keep its delegated traffic under the advertised limits. The information is advisory only and is not a guarantee, commitment or reservation of capacity.

today: RFC 9808 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2025. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC, and it supplements the Capability Objects of RFC 8008.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
When an upstream CDN (uCDN) delegates traffic to a downstream CDN (dCDN), it matters that the right amount is delegated. RFC 9808 defines a feedback mechanism that tells the delegator how much traffic may be sent. A service such as a request router can use that information in its delegation decisions.

The information is advisory. The RFC states that it does not represent a guarantee, commitment, or reservation of capacity. It adds two Capability Objects to those defined in Section 4 of RFC 8008, and registers matching CDNI Payload Types (a concept from RFC 8006).
sections.eli5: A shop that sends orders to a partner shop needs to know how many it can send. The partner's answer is only a helpful hint, not a promise.

sections.title: How Limits and Usage Fit Together
sections.content:
In normal operation the uCDN talks to the dCDN through an interface to learn the limits the dCDN has set. Limits are expressed as metrics such as bits per second or requests per second, and can be thought of as Not to Exceed (NTE) limits.

The dCDN should also give access to a Telemetry Source of near real-time metrics. The uCDN compares its current usage with the limits and adjusts delegation to stay under them. Pairing a limit with a corresponding Telemetry Source gives both parties an unambiguous definition.

Limits are valid for the Time to Live (TTL) given by the underlying transport, for example an HTTP Cache-Control header. The intent is a long-lived TTL and a reasonable peak utilization limit. If the transport cannot carry a TTL, it should be agreed out of band.
sections.eli5: The partner shop gives you a number and a scoreboard. You watch the scoreboard and slow down before you hit the number.

sections.title: The Telemetry Capability Object
sections.content:
The FCI.Telemetry Capability Object advertises a list of Telemetry Sources the dCDN makes available to the uCDN. Telemetry here means near real-time aggregated metrics of dCDN utilization, such as bits per second egress, specific to the uCDN and dCDN delegation relationship.

It has one mandatory property, sources, an array of Telemetry Source objects. Each source has a mandatory id (unique within the advertisement and consistent across advertisements), a mandatory type, a mandatory array of metrics, and an optional configuration object. Its structure depends on the source and is outside this document's scope; for the generic type it is defined out of band.

Each metric has a mandatory name, unique within its source, plus optional properties:

  • time-granularity: seconds the data represents, so 300 means the last 5 minutes.
  • data-percentile: the percentile the data represents. If absent, the data MUST be the mean over the time representation.
  • latency: seconds the data is behind real time, which helps the uCDN judge how long its adjustments take to show up.

The RFC notes that in multi-CDN chains a uCDN needs to aggregate dCDN usage with its own, otherwise delegated traffic becomes invisible to the content provider.
sections.eli5: A telemetry source is a scoreboard. Each line on it says what is being counted, over how long, and how old the number is.

sections.title: The CapacityLimits Capability Object
sections.content:
The FCI.CapacityLimits object lets the dCDN state delegation limits inside an FCI Capabilities advertisement. It has one mandatory property, limits, an array of CapacityLimit objects. Each limit is scoped to the footprint of the advertisement that contains it. Multiple limits MUST be combined with a logical AND, so the uCDN must respect all of them, not just the most specific one.

A CapacityLimit has these properties:

  • limit-type (mandatory): the units of the maximums.
  • maximum-hard (mandatory): the maximum capacity available for use.
  • maximum-soft (optional): a level at which the uCDN SHOULD reduce traffic before the hard limit. It MUST be less than maximum-hard, and if absent it equals maximum-hard.
  • id (optional): an identifier, unique among limit ids in the advertisement.
  • current (optional): inline current usage. This is NOT RECOMMENDED because it reduces cacheability; the intended method is a Telemetry Source.
  • telemetry-source (optional): maps the limit to a specific metric, using an id naming a Telemetry Source and a metric naming one of its metrics.
sections.eli5: Each limit says 'please stay under this number', and a softer 'start slowing down here' number. All the rules apply at the same time.

sections.title: Limit Types and Source Types
sections.content:
The valid limit-type values are those in the 'CDNI Capacity Limit Types' registry. The RFC lists six, chosen as the most relevant for traffic delegation between CDNs: egress (bits per second), requests (requests per second), storage-size (total bytes), storage-objects (count), sessions (count) and cache-size (total bytes).

For telemetry, the 'CDNI Telemetry Source Types' registry holds a single type at the time of writing: generic, a source-agnostic type for advertising generic data sources. Other types are expected to be specified later in a telemetry interface specification.
sections.eli5: The limits can count different things: data speed, number of requests, storage, or how many visitors are connected at once.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a JSON example of each object. In the telemetry example, a source capacity_metrics_region1 of type generic exposes a metric egress_5m with time-granularity 300, data-percentile 50 and latency 1500, alongside a second metric requests_5m.

In the limits example, a limit capacity_limit_region1 of type egress has a hard maximum of 50000000000 and a soft maximum of 25000000000, and its telemetry-source points at that source and its egress_5m metric. This is the link that makes the limit and the measurement refer to the same thing.
sections.eli5: The example says 'stay under this many bits per second, and here is the exact scoreboard line to check'.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered two CDNI Payload Types, FCI.Telemetry and FCI.CapacityLimits, both for the FCI interface. It also created two registries in the CDNI Parameters registry group: 'CDNI Telemetry Source Types' (initially generic) and 'CDNI Capacity Limit Types' (initially the six types above). Both use the Specification Required policy from RFC 8126, with guidelines for the designated expert, for example that a new type does not duplicate an existing one and is clearly justified.
sections.eli5: The names of the new message kinds and the lists of allowed limit and source types are written in an official public list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds no new security text of its own. It is in accordance with the CDNI Request Routing: Footprint and Capabilities Semantics, and so is subject to the security and privacy considerations in Section 7 of RFC 8008.
sections.eli5: It follows the same safety rules as the document it extends.
